title: Context Managers
description: The with statement, the __enter__/__exit__ protocol, and writing custom context managers for resource management.
objectives: Understand what problem the with statement solves
Implement a custom context manager with __enter__ and __exit__
Use contextlib for simpler context managers

content.heading: The with Statement and the Protocol
content.body:
The with statement guarantees that setup and cleanup code run around a block, even if an exception occurs inside it — the classic example is a file, which must be closed whether or not reading/writing it succeeds. Any object usable in a with statement is a context manager: it implements __enter__(self), called when entering the block (its return value becomes the as variable, if used), and __exit__(self, exc_type, exc_value, traceback), called when leaving the block, whether normally or via an exception.

If __exit__ returns a truthy value, any exception that occurred inside the with block is suppressed (treated as handled) rather than propagating further — a powerful but easy-to-misuse feature, since silently swallowing exceptions can hide real bugs if used carelessly.

content.heading: Writing Custom Context Managers
content.body: Any resource that needs reliable setup/teardown is a good candidate for a custom context manager: database connections, locks, timers, temporary state changes. Beyond writing a class with __enter__/__exit__, the contextlib module offers a much shorter alternative using a generator function decorated with @contextlib.contextmanager: code before the single yield acts as __enter__, the yielded value becomes the as variable, and code after yield (typically in a try/finally) acts as __exit__.

content.code:
import contextlib, time

class Timer:
    def __enter__(self):
        self.start = time.time()
        return self
    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc_value, traceback):
        print(f"Elapsed: {time.time() - self.start:.4f}s")
        return False   # do not suppress exceptions

with Timer():
    total = sum(range(100000))

@contextlib.contextmanager
def timer():
    start = time.time()
    yield
    print(f"Elapsed: {time.time() - start:.4f}s")

with timer():
    total = sum(range(100000))
content.explanation: Both the class-based Timer and the generator-based timer() achieve the same thing: guaranteed 'print elapsed time' cleanup, even if the code inside the with block raised an exception.

keyPoints: with guarantees setup/cleanup even when an exception occurs inside the block
__exit__ returning a truthy value suppresses the exception it was given
@contextlib.contextmanager turns a simple generator function into a context manager
commonMistakes: Implementing only __enter__ and forgetting __exit__, breaking the with protocol
Accidentally suppressing exceptions by returning a truthy value from __exit__ unintentionally
Using a plain try/finally everywhere instead of a reusable context manager for a repeated setup/teardown pattern
